analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with high-risk pools, health savings accounts, malpractice damage caps, and interstate insurance sales.
analysis.headline: A single Republican bill to repeal the ACA and substitute a replacement never gained a cosponsor and died in its first committee referral without any hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the Affordable Care Act in its entirety, then rebuild pieces of it. People with pre-existing conditions could no longer be denied or charged more when they enroll, but insurers could again sell stripped-down policies across state lines, and medical malpractice payouts for pain and suffering would be capped at $250,000. It also expands tax-advantaged health savings accounts and creates association health plans for small businesses.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income savers who benefit most from expanded health savings accounts; small business associations; insurers who could sell lighter-regulated policies across state lines; doctors and medical product makers facing capped malpractice awards.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, insurers, doctors, drug and device makers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Affordable Care Act effective as of its enactment, restoring the pre-2010 legal landscape, per the CRS summary [S2].
Keeps a ban on annual and lifetime coverage caps and prevents unjust cancellation of coverage [S3].
Caps noneconomic damages in medical malpractice cases at $250,000 and shortens the window to sue to as little as one year after discovery [S3].
Expands health savings account eligibility to Medicare Part A beneficiaries, veterans with service-connected disabilities, Indian Health Service users, and TRICARE-eligible individuals [S3].
Requires every state to run a reinsurance program or high-risk pool to cover the cost of medically expensive patients [S2].
Rewards states that reduce premiums or the uninsured rate with federal awards [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Patients badly harmed by medical negligence, who could lose most compensation for pain and suffering; and people who relied on ACA subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and guaranteed-issue protections, whose coverage support would vanish.
analysis.who_pays_short: Malpractice victims and people who gained ACA coverage

drawbacks.text: Removes the prohibition on preexisting condition exclusions in the individual market, replacing guaranteed coverage with a state pool or reinsurance mechanism [S2].
Caps malpractice payouts for pain and suffering at $250,000 regardless of injury severity and makes it much harder to win punitive damages against medical product makers [S3].
Allows insurers to sell coverage governed by a single 'primary state' into every other state, letting them bypass each state's benefit mandates and consumer protections [S3].
Repeals the ACA's Medicaid expansion funding and premium tax credits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protects a few ACA consumer protections but replaces a system of subsidies and guaranteed issue with high-risk pools and capped malpractice awards, shifting risk onto the sickest patients and people who lost coverage subsidies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in eight House committees and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: It was referred to eight committees on the day it was introduced and sent to subcommittees, none of which acted on it [S5].
It never gained a single cosponsor in the 113th Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's failure preserved the Affordable Care Act's subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and consumer protections in place at the time; no constituency changed position because no action occurred.

for.name: Rep. Sean P. Duffy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it as a full repeal-and-replace alternative to the ACA.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever took place, and no other member signed on, so the partisan split can't be measured.

industries.note: Insurers would gain the ability to sell lightly regulated policies across state lines and avoid guaranteed-issue rules, but lose ACA-related subsidies and enrollment. Patients could face narrower coverage and fewer consumer protections.

industries.industry: Medical malpractice insurers and health care providers
industries.note: A $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages and tighter lawsuit timelines would cut their liability exposure. Injured patients would absorb the difference.
The bill largely shields FDA-approved products from punitive damages, reducing litigation risk even for products later found defective.
